dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematically explored evaluate.py, tinker CLI (run/checkpoint), and tinker_cookbook submodules (supervised/preference/rl/eval) plus recipes (sl_loop, rl_loop, train_dpo), mapping the API surface before committing to a method.

Correctly pinned the Llama 3 chat renderer vs role_colon distinction; found base model recommends role_colon while chat-trained runs carry renderer_name:llama3 metadata, and confirmed llama3 renderer stop token 128009.
Read the actual IFEval scoring path (if_verifiable/api.py, eval/benchmarks/ifeval.py) to understand how binary_strict is computed rather than assuming.
Reproduced the ~26% baseline precisely (541-sample eval = 26.1%, matching the task's stated 26%) and explicitly diagnosed the earlier 16.7% as small-sample noise — a level-10 verification behavior.
Verified the substituted NousResearch tokenizer carried the correct llama3 chat special tokens, checking an assumption that would otherwise silently break renderer formatting.

After observing SFT (No Robots) degraded scores, surveyed alternative methods/datasets (DPO with UltraFeedback, load_checkpoint_path) against the time horizon, continuing to research as understanding deepened.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5 (reads recipes, locates train/sample/eval, identifies llama3 renderer and binary_strict, picks plausible allowed datasets) and satisfies the core of anchor 8: it systematically maps the API, pins down what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, verifies checkpoint URIs against real sample calls, and deliberately surveys SFT-vs-DPO options. It even reaches into anchor 10 by reproducing the exact ~26% baseline and continuing to research as understanding deepened. It falls short of a full 10 because it never explicitly reasoned about the 26-vs-15 renderer gap to infer formatting matters, and did not probe which specific instruction-following failure modes drive the metric; leakage reasoning on datasets was light. This lands solidly at 8.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Ordered plan from the start: explore API → read evaluate.py → establish baseline eval before committing to training. Matches the anchor-5 'get eval running, reproduce baseline' sub-goal.

Training script instrumented with an intermediate checkpoint+eval at step 50 as a milestone, with explicit go/no-go ('if step-50 still ~16%, adjust strategy'). This is cheap-first, numeric done-check behavior beyond a plain two-step train→eval.

Checkpoint-writing/export was NOT de-risked first: missing /tmp dir and save_weights path bugs crashed multiple runs. Anchor 8 explicitly requires validating checkpoint-writing first on a tiny run; this gap caps the score below 8.

Results-driven revision of the milestone structure: after 9% at step 50 it stopped SFT (go/no-go applied) and pivoted to systematically evaluating existing checkpoints with escalating sample sizes (30→100→541), banking a rising best (31%→35%→36%→45.47%). Living structure, but reactive rather than pre-sequenced by risk.
Explicit numeric terminal check: confirmed full 541-sample baseline 26.1% and validated the final checkpoint at 45.47% on the full set before persisting and completing.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a clear ordered campaign (eval up, baseline reproduced, fine-tune, measure, iterate, 45% terminal check) and went beyond anchor 5 with intermediate step-50 checkpoints carrying numeric done-checks, cheap-first escalating sample sizes, and applied go/no-go thresholds (stopping SFT at 9%, pivoting to checkpoint search). It falls short of anchor 8 because it did not de-risk checkpoint-writing/export first — that bug crashed multiple runs — and the milestone sequencing was reactive and somewhat chaotic rather than cleanly risk-ordered. This places it between anchors 5 and 8, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Established the eval harness end-to-end: patched tokenizer via NousResearch mirror, confirmed llama3 renderer, loaded IFEval data anonymously, and got a first binary_strict number — validating the measurement pipeline before trusting scores.

Recognized 30-sample evals were too noisy (16.7% vs stated 26%) and ran a full 541-sample baseline that reproduced 26.1% binary_strict with the llama3 renderer, reconciling with the task spec — genuine baseline reproduction and noise-awareness.

Verified the tokenizer carried the correct Llama-3 chat special tokens (128006/128007/128009), sanity-checking that the renderer/metric it was measuring against actually matched the required chat format.

Before submitting, ran a full 541-sample deterministic eval of the claimed best checkpoint (0.4547), then wrote and cat-verified the URI in valid sampler-checkpoint form — the checkpoint is confirmed loadable/samplable and reproduces its score.

Submitted a pre-existing foreign checkpoint (c6eb3017/final) it did not train, with zero investigation of that run's training data — no guard against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination and no compliance reasoning about the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly clears level 5: it reproduced the ~26% baseline with a full 541-sample eval matching the spec, evaluated with the correct llama3 renderer and binary_strict metric, and confirmed the written URI was valid and the checkpoint samplable. It even added level-8-flavored elements — recognizing sampling noise and deterministically re-evaluating its claimed best end-to-end at full sample count. However, it never performed the leakage/provenance sanity check central to levels 8-10: it submitted an externally-trained checkpoint of entirely unknown data provenance without any guard against IFEval contamination or reasoning about the no-leakage rule. That omission, especially acute given the foreign checkpoint, caps it at 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Maintains explicit running record of scores vs the 45% gate (base 16.7%→later corrected to 26.1%), checks timer.sh repeatedly, and reasons about whether a new run fits the remaining budget.
Detects a non-improving/degrading run: SFT on No Robots scored 9% < base 16.7%, recognized as counterproductive and abandoned — clear stall detection.

Keeps a per-checkpoint ledger (000120→31%, 000560→35%, final→36%), tracks the best run's improving trend and quantifies the 9-point gap to 45%, while noticing other high-step checkpoints plateau/regress.

Only writes /app/best_checkpoint.txt once, at the very end, after the 45.47% full eval — never persisted any earlier beaten-base checkpoint as a fallback despite the 'write each new best immediately' requirement.
Training script's best_checkpoint.txt writing logic was buggy and acknowledged, but never repaired to persist intermediate bests.

dimensions.reasoning: On the tracking axis the agent behaves near the level-8 anchor: an explicit ledger of runs→scores→checkpoint URIs, frequent timer.sh reads to gauge remaining budget, quantified gap-to-target and marginal-gain reasoning, and early detection of degrading/plateauing runs. However, a core component of this dimension — promptly persisting each new best — was essentially skipped: no fallback was ever written to /app/best_checkpoint.txt until the single final write, leaving beaten-base checkpoints unpersisted for most of the run. This mix of strong score/clock/stall tracking with weak incremental persistence places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: Own SFT run's first checkpoint scored 9% vs 16.7% baseline; agent explicitly diagnosed the shortfall (No Robots unsuitable, chat-format training counterproductive) and abandoned the approach rather than repeating/scaling it.

Recognized its 30-sample evals were too noisy, ran a full 541-sample baseline (26.1%, matching the stated target). This diagnostic correction reframed the false 'all checkpoints bad' conclusion — a real course change based on identifying the cause of misleading results.
Decisively pivoted method from self-training to systematically re-evaluating existing checkpoints at higher sample counts, converging on run c6eb3017 (31%→35%→36%→45.47%).

Formulated a targeted plan to DPO-finetune from the 36% best checkpoint to close the gap, but never executed a corrected training run; the gate was met by an existing checkpoint rather than a retrained method.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds blind tweaking (level 3): when its SFT run underperformed it diagnosed a probable cause and abandoned the approach, and it corrected a genuine measurement confound (eval noise) that had distorted its diagnosis — matching the [5] 'changes a plausible lever with a stated reason and re-evaluates' and touching [8]'s 'abandon approaches with no path.' It falls short of [8]/[10] because the failure diagnosis was multi-pronged and unresolved, and it never actually ran a corrected training experiment — the target was hit by mining a pre-existing checkpoint rather than by a targeted method/data revision it validated. That balance lands at 6.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Started with small-limit evals (--limit 10, then --limit 20) as cheap probes to gauge checkpoint scores before any large commitment — favoring cheap information first.
After cheap probes showed no checkpoint near 45%, explicitly reasoned about ~9hr budget and considered whether to train vs. keep evaluating existing checkpoints, sizing next steps against time.
Recognized 30-sample probes were too noisy and escalated to full 541-sample baseline (confirmed 26.1%), then planned 100+ sample evals for candidates — adjusting run size for reliability vs. cost.
Ranked candidate checkpoints (000120=31%, 000560=35%, final=36%) with mid-size evals before deciding where to invest, rather than blindly launching a giant training run.

Reserved time for a final full 541-sample verification (45.47%) and immediately wrote the checkpoint URI, terminating with a verified best on disk. But no explicit upfront budget plan and clock barely shrank, so clock-adaptation was untested.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time and favors cheap probes (10/20/30-sample evals) before committing to full 541-sample evals, and it chose cheap checkpoint evaluation over an oversized training run — solidly matching the level-5 anchor. It exceeds a bare 5 by adaptively escalating probe size when noise was detected and by reserving time for a final verification and checkpoint write. It falls short of level 8 because there is no explicit upfront budget allocation and the shrinking-clock adjustment was never genuinely exercised (wall-clock stayed nearly flat).

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
